extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of world history
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesizing broad sweeps of political, social, economic, and cultural history for a general audience, emphasizing causes, consequences, and readable interpretation rather than exhaustive specialist detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat national/romantic events as ornament, not foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: “For every country has such cherished national events. They are the ornamental tapestry of history, and no part of the building.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let celebrated battles, national myths, or romanticized individual episodes dominate an account of longer-term historical development; present them as prominent but largely decorative elements that sit atop deeper social, economic, and institutional structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize underlying forces over artistic productions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Artistic productions, unlike philosophical thought and scientific discovery, are the ornaments and expression rather than the creative substance of history.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing what ‘mattered’ historically, emphasize structural forces (political, economic, technological, institutional) as drivers; treat art and artistic achievement as expressive indicators of broader conditions rather than primary causal agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use material culture and architecture as social indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages describing the rise of Gothic cathedrals, abbeys, and town buildings and linking them to craftsmen, church wealth, and later royal/merchant patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and use architectural and material developments (e.g., cathedral-building, town halls, fortifications) as evidence of social organization, economic capacity, and the relationship between church, crown, and emerging urban classes; note shifts in patronage (church → kings/merchants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze towns as proto-state actors with broad social functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of medieval towns: guild regulation of trade, councils administering social problems, municipal granaries, price tariffs, municipal finance (annuities), fortifications, fire brigades, and provision of poor relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat towns not merely as market places but as administrative bodies performing many functions later associated with states; evaluate urban institutions (guilds, councils, charters) for their role in economic regulation, social welfare, defense, and credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider shifts in trade and navigation as geopolitical pivots
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the shift of European focus from Mediterranean/Levant to the Atlantic following exploration and discovery (Columbus, Vasco da Gama, Magellan) and consequent changes in centers of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining major shifts in international power, foreground changes in trade routes, navigational technology, and discovery (compass, ship types, new sea routes) as central drivers that re-orient economic and political centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value historical writings for revealing contemporary mentalities
rubrics_metrics.description: “The enduring value of these books lies in the clear idea they give us of the quality and limitations of the ruling minds of this age. Their atmosphere was his atmosphere.” (on Machiavelli)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate primary and contemporary political writings primarily for what they reveal about the beliefs, assumptions, and mentalities of their authors and times; use such works as windows into ruling ideas rather than merely as policy manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret political treatises by their normative assumptions about power
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization of Machiavelli: “His ruling thought, his great contribution to political literature, was that the moral obligations upon ordinary men cannot bind princes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing political theory or advice literature, identify and make explicit the normative premises (e.g., about morality, ends-justifying-means) that underlie prescriptions for rulers; situate these premises within the political environment that produced them.
